author: Bryan A. Garner
introFa: کتاب «Garner's Modern English Usage» نوشته Bryan A. Garner یکی از منابع ارزشمند و معتبر برای یادگیری زبان انگلیسی در سطح C2 است. این اثر با ساختاری منسجم و غنی، شما را در تسلط بر واژگان و درک مطلب یاری می‌کند.
readingTipsFa: پیش از مطالعه هر بخش از کتاب «Garner's Modern English Usage»، نگاهی سریع به تیترها و ساختار آن بیندازید.
واژگان و اصطلاحات جدید را در زمینه و بافت جمله یادداشت کنید تا در حافظه بلندمدت تثبیت شوند.

content: unaware of its nature! He also discusses (In) Back Of, but again without mentioning that it is unknown in Britain, where we do say “in front of” but “behind”. Other differences he might have mentioned are Faculty (in America, the teaching staff of a college, etc.; in Britain, a department or division of a university), and, in the same ﬁeld, Dormitory (in Britain, a communal bedroom; in America, a building housing students, what in Britain would be a hall of residence). Garner is, in my view, wrong to say Earth (the planet), Sun (our star) and Moon (Earth’s natural satellite) should be lower-cased. They are just as much proper names as other planets (Mars), stars (Sirius) or Deimos (a satellite of Mars), and should be capitalized. I also disagree that Frankenstein can now be used for a monster, rather than the man who created the monster. He is also wrong to approve of that dreadful term Xmas, giving as his reason what I would call good reason to condemn it, that the X is actually the Greek chi, the ﬁrst letter of Christos. Among things Garner might have mentioned but doesn’t is the irritating, ignorant practice of saying “autobiography” for biography (which would n’t happen if people knew what auto means); the change in the meaning of impertinent (literally “irrelevant”, but now more often used for bad-mannered, so that non-pertinent has come into use for the original meaning); jaywalking (almost unknown in Britain, which has never had any laws about pedestrians crossing the road); nervy (in America, meaning bold, conﬁdent, “having lots of nerve”, but in Britain, almost the opposite: nervous, jumpy); nipple (having only an anatomical meaning in Britain, but in America, meaning a teat); and the confusion of silicon and silicone (as soon as silicon chips came into the news, people were calling them silicone chips, though they are, of course, completely different substances). And there is no entry on toilet and the American practice of saying bathroom for private facilities and restroom for public ones. Under Class Distinctions, Garner discusses U and non-U but, like most commentators, fails to mention the most signiﬁcant point: that, while many assumed that the U would use genteel, euphemistic terms, the non-U crude, vulgar ones, it was, very often, the other way round, with the U term being the blunter. Garner says gay and lesbian is “peculiarly redundant”, as lesbians are gay women. I have, however, never known a woman be called gay; the problem, which Garner doesn’t address, is that there is a speciﬁc term, lesbian, for a homosexual woman, but not for such a man, and gay seems to be assuming that position. Nor does he address the confusion caused by homo meaning man, though in homosexual, it actually means “the same” and can be used of either sex. To my great pleasure, Garner makes the distinction between Great Britain and United Kingdom clear, and that the “Great” isn’t boastful, simply referring to geographical size. He also stoutly defends the infer/imply distinction, and, to my delight, says that the names of bodies should be spelt as they spell them themselves; I and others fought a long battle to convince Time magazine there was no British institution called the Labor Party. But he should note that the British shortening of mackintosh for a raincoat is mac, not “mack”. I was surprised to read that Monacan, not Monegasque, is the standard term for a citizen of Monaco; I have always understood it to be the latter, and never heard of the former. I was equally surprised to hear San Marino was “near” Italy when Italy surrounds it! There is an excellent essay on a favourite linguistic phenomenon of mine, mondegreens (as when many people, including me, thought Jimi Hendrix’s “Excuse me while I kiss the sky” was “Excuse me while I kiss this guy”). The discussion of Native American is interesting, but I would have expected references from Aleut, Eskimo, Indian and (a term not mentioned at all) Inuit. I have never heard of Garner’s ﬁrst deﬁnition of planetarium, “a model of the solar system”, and his second, “a building or room for projecting images of the solar system” is wrong; it is in fact a dome on the inside of which are projected exact images of the night sky, including planets, stars, etc., as they would appear from Earth. In the comprehensive (eight pages!) essay on punctuation, Garner says the British call quotation marks “inverted commas”. Not this Briton; I agree with whoever it was (Eric Partridge, I think) who said they are neither inverted nor commas. And I much prefer the American practice of using double marks (“[. . .]”) to the British one of using single ones (“[. . .]”), simply on grounds of visibility. Garner discusses the phenomenon of words acquiring wrong meanings from their accidental resemblance to others, but only in individual entries like those on careen for career, enormity for bigness or largeness and scarify for frighten or alarm. He also discusses transportation with no mention of or reference from the usual British term, transport. The difference is sometimes attributed to the American liking for long words, but in fact is more likely to be because in Britain, transportation had a bound-for-Botany-Bay air, being what was done to convicts sent to Australia and elsewhere. other language-related terms, an interesting timeline of books on usage starting in 1758 (some very obscure, while some well-known ones are missing, including Keith Waterhouse’s books on newspaper English and Lynne Truss’s classic on punctuation, Eats, Shoots and Leaves), a select bibliography, a select index of writers quoted or mentioned and, on the back endpaper, a pronunciation guide. There is far more to this book than I have been able to mention. It is a stupendous achievement for which we should be grateful. You have to like a book which tells you whether spaghetti and meatballs takes a singular or plural verb! But I fear Kingsley Amis was right when he said that such works provide not description but prescription: not English as she is spoken (or written), but English as she should be spoke or written, and that those who most need such works are the least likely to consult them. Kinnahan Cambridge University Press Cambridge 2016 xxi  458 pp. ISBN 978 1 107 13756 1 (print); ISBN 978 1 31687 9 (e-book) £64.99 $110 (print); $88 (e-book) Keywords Twentieth century, United States of America, Women, Poetry Review DOI 10.1108/RR-04-2017-0104 Oftentimes a book title is a marker of convenience, signalling the marketplace position of its contents rather than accurately reﬂecting the diversity within the book. The title under review here is one such title. The ambition of a singular historical trajectory subtending the words “A History” is not the aim of this title. The positioning work undertaken in the Preface demonstrates that histories are plural; “history as multiple and layered, maintaining a keen awareness of the impossibility of a singular, comprehensive history of such poetic activity on the part of women writing between 1900 and 2000” (p. 17). The contextualizing provided in this Preface also anticipates the querying of validity which is, even now, still levelled at scholarship and creative endeavours foregrounding the work of women. In anticipation of this, editor Linda A. Kinnahan states: Adopting the critical stance that maintains a separate attention upon women poets, their poetic connections to one another, and their poetical developments, these essays further insist upon the signiﬁcance of moving beyond and unsettling “the picture” by reading outside the frames of literary histories we have inherited, most often constructed around (and by) the work of men (p. 17). The book presents 23 chapters in six broadly themed parts. The contents clearly set out the themes and chapters, making it easily navigable for the long read or the short dip. The thematic sections facilitate readings of the poetry therein by eschewing the “periods” and “movements” with which the vagaries of time are so often measured in academic literary scholarship. One of the advantages of this approach is the lifting of categories with which the reader may be familiar, allowing the poetries to be approached if not afresh then at least with a fresh lens. In Part I: Mappings and Chronologies, four chapters establish the scope of this volume. The concept of mapping enables an overview of the poetries which later chapters explore in depth. Chapter 1 is written by Linda A. Kinnahan, who offers an exploration of The Category of the “Woman Poet” and uses the opening chapter as, to quote the subtitle, “An Introduction, by Way of Mapping”. In Chapter 2, Reading American Poetry by Woman, poet and scholar Rachel Blau DuPlessis continues the mapping approach, focusing on poetry by women as a reception strategy for reading (and writing). Chapters 3 and 4 provide chronologies, American Women Poets, 1900-1950, and American Women Poets, 1950-2000, respectively. Part II comprises ﬁve chapters under the heading Ethnicity, Race, and Identity. A chapter is devoted to each of the following: Native American Women Poets, Asian American Women Poets, Chicana/Latina Women Poets, African American Women Poets and Jewish American Women Poets. Part III presents under the somewhat mysterious sounding heading Material Formations. The ﬁve chapters here share themes which suggest a situatedness of the poetries under discussion: Chapter 10 looks at Social Critique, while Chapter 11 explores Little Magazines and the Gendered, Racialised Discourse of Women’s Poetry.
